summaries.summary: Flickr tags and GPS coordinates make georeferenced photos a source of environmental information, though Flickr's usefulness for characterizing the natural environment is less understood.
Flickr tags capture valuable ecological information, but ecologists have mostly used social media manually, with BIBREF7 finding promising bag-of-words prediction results.
The paper hypothesizes that vector space embeddings better utilize ecological information in Flickr tags and naturally integrate structured numerical and categorical environmental data.
Off-the-shelf GloVe performed poorly, requiring spatial smoothing and term selection, while embeddings with structured scientific information substantially improved predictions.
The paper is organized with existing work, the embedding model, experimental results, and conclusions in subsequent sections.
Low-dimensional vector space embeddings are effective across applications, and the paper builds on GloVe, which captures linear regularities of word-word co-occurrence.
GloVe's objective uses co-occurrence counts, vocabulary size, biases, and a weighting function, with INLINEFORM9 usually fixed to 100 and INLINEFORM10 to 0.75.
Prior work learns vector space representations from structured data and combines word embeddings with knowledge graphs, lexicons, and semantic categories.
BIBREF31 used principal component analysis and stacked autoencoders to learn low-dimensional city neighbourhood representations from census data for predicting attributes such as crime.
BIBREF32 learns word embeddings from shared geographic locations, whereas this paper uses textual descriptions to learn vectors representing geographic locations.
Several methods use word embedding models to learn Points-of-Interest representations for predicting user visits, often without considering textual information.
This work focuses on representing locations from Flickr tags plus numerical and categorical features from scientific datasets.
BIBREF7 found georeferenced Flickr tags supplement scientific environmental data, but concatenating bag-of-words and structured feature vectors is far from optimal.
BIBREF44 is the only work generating embeddings for Flickr tags, focusing on word meaning rather than representing locations.
The section introduces an embedding model combining Flickr tags and structured scientific information to represent a set of locations INLINEFORM0.
Parameters INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 control components constraining locations by Flickr tags, numerical features, and shared categories.
The authors collected tags and meta-data of 70 million Flickr photos with coordinates in Europe, uploaded before the end of September 2015.
Tag weighting follows BIBREF7, combining a Gaussian kernel for spatial proximity with Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI).
A Gaussian kernel weights tag occurrences by distance from a location rather than simply counting occurrences within a fixed radius.
The weighting uses a fixed threshold INLINEFORM0, Haversine distance, bandwidth INLINEFORM4, user-level counting, and PPMI from INLINEFORM12 values.
The paragraph presents an equation labeled INLINEFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is the set of all tags, and INLINEFORM1 is the set of locations.
Tag selection uses Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to focus on important tags and reduce individual or group-specific tag effects.
The KL score uses probabilities INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM3, with INLINEFORM5 estimated using Bayesian smoothing.
INLINEFORM0 controls smoothing and is tuned in experiments, while INLINEFORM1 uses maximum likelihood estimation.
Location embedding uses a close GloVe variant where tag occurrences are context words and locations have vectors INLINEFORM3.
The objective uses INLINEFORM0 scores and negative examples, sampling tags near location INLINEFORM5 plus negative examples for computational feasibility.
The work uses nine numerical features and 180 categorical features, including CORINE land cover classes and 116 SoilGrids soil types.
Numerical features are predicted from location vectors using a linear mapping with vector INLINEFORM1 and bias term INLINEFORM2.
INLINEFORM0 is the set of all numerical features, and INLINEFORM1 is the z-score normalized value of feature INLINEFORM2 for location INLINEFORM3.
Categorical features constrain locations in the same category to be close, with each category type INLINEFORM0 represented as vector INLINEFORM1.
The method from BIBREF7 is the main baseline, enabling direct evaluation with the same structured datasets, tag weighting scheme, and three evaluation tasks.
The first task predicts the distribution of 100 species across Europe using Natura 2000 as ground truth, with binary classification over 26,425 distinct sites INLINEFORM0.
The second task predicts soil type as binary classification using the same locations INLINEFORM0, without using soil type features to generate embeddings.
The third task predicts CORINE land cover classes at levels 1, 2 and level 3 as binary classification using INLINEFORM0, without CORINE features in embeddings.
The authors additionally consider the following regression tasks.

One regression task predicts 5 climate related features using INLINEFORM0, without climate features in embeddings: average precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, water vapor pressure, and wind speed.
Another regression task predicts landscape beauty opinions in Britain using ScenicOrNot, with INLINEFORM0 comprising 191 605 rated locations having a georeferenced Flickr photo within 1 km.

Experiments use SVMs and SVR with BIBREF53, two-thirds training, one-sixth testing, one-sixth tuning, Adagrad with 30 iterations, tuned dimensions, parameters, discretization cut-offs, top 100 000 tags, 1km radius, capped negative examples, F1 score, and Spearman INLINEFORM9.
The authors define EGEL variants EGEL-Tags, EGEL-Tags+NS, EGEL-KL(Tags+NS), and EGEL-All, plus baselines BOW-Tags, BOW-KL(Tags), BOW-All, and GloVe.

Binary classification results use average precision, average recall and macro average F1 score, while regression results use mean absolute error and Spearman INLINEFORM0 correlation; EGEL-All outperforms baselines for all tasks.
Embeddings are consistently useful only with tags and structured datasets, while BOW-Tags sometimes performs best and term selection may lose information from highly specific rare tags.
Figure TABREF29 shows GloVe outperforms bag-of-words for large corpora and underperforms for smaller corpora, an issue alleviated by negative examples.

The paper proposes geographic location embeddings from Flickr tags, numerical environmental features, and categorical information, with substantial improvements over baselines on natural environment prediction tasks.
